subject: humanities
passage: When sound films arrived in the late 1920s, audiences flocked to hear actors speak and sing on screen. Many film histories describe the change simply as progress: movies gained a powerful new tool, and nothing important was lost.
passage_b: Early sound recording came with real costs. Because cameras were noisy, they were often shut inside soundproof booths and could hardly move, and actors had to stay close to hidden microphones. As a result, many early sound films look stiff compared with the flowing camera work of the best silent films made just a few years before.
stem: Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the view of sound films in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that early sound films improved on silent films in every way
choices.B: By arguing that audiences preferred silent films to sound films
choices.C: By pointing out that the change to sound also limited how films could be shot
choices.D: By suggesting that actors refused to work near microphones

explanation.why: Text 1 says film histories treat sound as pure progress in which "nothing important was lost." Text 2 says sound "came with real costs": cameras "could hardly move" and actors had to stay near microphones, making films "look stiff." So Text 2 would point to a loss Text 1 ignores.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Text 2 says early sound films often looked stiff compared with silent films, so it does not see them as better in every way.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Text 2 discusses how films were made, not what audiences preferred; Text 1 says audiences "flocked" to sound films.
explanation.C: Correct. Text 2 explains that cameras in soundproof booths could barely move, a real limit on filmmaking.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Text 2 says actors had to stay close to microphones, not that they refused to.
